summary: Eberhard Bethge (1909-2000 CE) was a German theologian and pastor of the Confessing Church, the student, closest friend, and later literary executor of Dietrich Bonhoeffer. He was the principal recipient of Bonhoeffer's letters from Tegel prison, including the 1944 letters containing the late theological ideas; he preserved and edited them and first published them as Widerstand und Ergebung (1951, English Letters and Papers from Prison), and he wrote the standard biography Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1967).
description:
Eberhard Bethge was born in 1909 at Warchau in the Prussian Province of Saxony (near Magdeburg) and trained for the ministry in the Confessing Church, the church body that resisted the alignment of the German Evangelical Church with National Socialism. He studied under Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906-1945) at the Confessing Church's illegal preachers' seminary at Finkenwalde, and the two became close friends and collaborators; Bethge later married Renate Schleicher, a niece of Bonhoeffer, so that he was also connected to Bonhoeffer's family by marriage. Through the years of the church struggle and the Second World War Bethge was Bonhoeffer's closest correspondent and confidant.

After Bonhoeffer's arrest in 1943 and imprisonment at the Tegel military prison in Berlin, Bethge was the principal recipient of the letters Bonhoeffer wrote from prison, including the series of letters in 1944 that contain the fragmentary late ideas for which the prison writings became known, among them a 'world come of age,' a 'religionless Christianity,' and a God who is 'pushed out of the world onto the cross.' Bethge preserved these letters, several of which were smuggled out of the prison, through the end of the war and Bonhoeffer's execution at the Flossenbuerg concentration camp on 9 April 1945. He then edited the letters and theological notes and first published them in German as Widerstand und Ergebung ('Resistance and Submission') in 1951; the collection appeared in English as Letters and Papers from Prison and became one of the most widely read theological works of the twentieth century.

As Bonhoeffer's literary executor Bethge devoted much of his life to editing, transmitting, and interpreting Bonhoeffer's writings, and he wrote the large biography Dietrich Bonhoeffer, first published in German in 1967 (English translation 1970, revised English edition 2000), which scholars treat as the standard account of Bonhoeffer's life. He continued as a pastor, teacher, and interpreter of Bonhoeffer until his death in 2000. This entry records Bethge's role in preserving, editing, and publishing the prison letters and in writing the biography as matters of historical report; it presents the theological ideas of the prison letters as Bonhoeffer's attributed late reflections, and it records that Bethge, as editor, preserved and arranged the prison fragments without systematising them into a finished theology. Interpretive judgments about the meaning of the prison theology are attributed to Bethge and to later scholarship, not adjudicated by the editor.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes Eberhard Bethge on Christian terms (neutrality #6). Bethge's roles as Bonhoeffer's student and friend, as recipient of the Tegel prison letters, as the editor who first published them as Widerstand und Ergebung (1951), and as the author of the standard biography are stated as historical fact. The theological ideas of the prison letters ('world come of age,' 'religionless Christianity,' the God 'pushed out of the world onto the cross') are attributed to Dietrich Bonhoeffer and to the letters themselves and are flagged as fragmentary late reflections, not endorsed or adjudicated (neutrality #1, #2), consistent with the letters-and-papers-from-prison entry, which this entry answers.

HONESTY / status and confidence: this entry is DRAFT and, on the sourcing available, tops out at reviewed rather than verified. The three sources are twentieth- and twenty-first-century proprietary works and were NOT read line by line for the load-bearing claims; they are verified to exist and be on-topic and are rated MEDIUM. Bethge's own Dietrich Bonhoeffer: A Biography (Fortress, 2000) is both the standard biography and the primary editorial witness, since Bethge was the recipient of the 1944 letters and the first editor of the collection. John W. de Gruchy's Daring, Trusting Spirit: Bonhoeffer's Friend Eberhard Bethge (Fortress, 2005) is the scholarly biography of Bethge himself. The critical edition of Letters and Papers from Prison (DBWE volume 8, Fortress, 2010), edited by de Gruchy, documents in its editorial apparatus Bethge's role as recipient and first editor and the 1951 publication of Widerstand und Ergebung; the open editor's introduction PDF was located but could not be read verbatim (encoded PDF), so no verbatim phrase is claimed from it.
